en: Sutta Nipāta 3.10 Kokālikasutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.”
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhu Kokālika:
“Do not speak thus, Kokālika; do not speak thus, Kokālika.
Set your mind at rest regarding Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”
“Pesalā are Sāriputta and Moggallāna!
A second time...
and a third time, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, although the Blessed One is trustworthy and reliable to me, nevertheless Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.
A third time the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhu Kokālika:
“Do not say so, Kokālika! Do not say so, Kokālika!”
“Kokālika, direct your mind with confidence toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna;
Sāriputta and Moggallāna are virtuous.
Then the bhikkhu Kokālika rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Not long after the monk Kokālika had departed, his entire body became covered with boils the size of mustard seeds;
having been the size of mustard seeds, they became the size of mung beans; having been the size of mung beans, they became the size of chickpeas;
having been the size of chickpeas, they became the size of jujube stones; and having been the size of jujube stones, they became the size of jujubes.
Having become the size of jujube fruits, they became the size of myrobalan fruits; having become the size of myrobalan fruits, they became the size of bamboo sprouts;
having become the size of bamboo sprouts, they became the size of wood-apple fruits; having become the size of wood-apple fruits, they burst open, and pus and blood flowed out.
Then the bhikkhu Kokālika died from that very affliction.
Having died, because he had harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the bhikkhu Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma Hell.
Then, when the night had advanced, Brahmā Sahampati, of surpassing beauty, [illuminated] the entire Jeta’s Grove.
Having illuminated [the world], he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Brahmā Sahampati said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has passed away."
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has passed away and has been reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said.
Having spoken thus, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, during this night, when the night was far spent, Brahmā Sahampati approached me...
[as before] ...This, bhikkhus, is what Brahmā Sahampati said. Having said this, he circumambulated me keeping me to his right and vanished right there.”
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One:
“Bhante, how long indeed is the lifespan in the Paduma hell?
“The lifespan in the Paduma hell, bhikkhu, is long.”
"It is not easy to calculate it as 'this many years,' or 'this many hundreds of years,' or 'this many thousands of years,' or 'this many hundreds of thousands of years.
"But, Bhante, is it possible to give a simile?
"It is possible, bhikkhus," the Blessed One said.

“Bhikkhu, it is just as if there were a Kosalan cartload of twenty measures of sesame seeds. If a man were to remove a single seed from it at the end of every hundred years, that Kosalan cartload of twenty measures of sesame seeds would, by this means, more quickly reach exhaustion and termination than one *abbuda* hell would last.
Bhikkhu, just as twenty *abbuda* hells are equal to one *nirabbuda* hell.”
Just as, bhikkhu, twenty *nirabbuda* hells are equal to one *ababa* hell;
just as, bhikkhu, twenty *ababa* hells are equal to one *aṭaṭa* hell;
just as, bhikkhu, twenty *aṭaṭa* hells are equal to one *ahaha* hell.
“Just as, bhikkhu, twenty Aṭaṭa hells are equal to one Kumuda hell;
just as, bhikkhu, twenty Kumuda hells are equal to one Sogandhika hell;
just as, bhikkhu, twenty Sogandhika hells are equal to one Uppalaka hell.”
“Just as, monk, twenty Uppalaka hells are equal to one Puṇḍarīka hell;
and just as, monk, twenty Puṇḍarīka hells are equal to one Paduma hell—
it was into this Paduma hell, monk, that the monk Kokālika was reborn after harboring a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
"For when a person is born..."
An axe is born in the mouth by which the fool cuts himself when speaking ill-spoken words.
He who praises one who should be blamed,
or blames one who should be praised,
gathers misfortune with his own mouth.

Even if one should lose everything, including one's very self,
this alone is the greater loss:
to harbor a mind of malice toward the Sugatas.
For one hundred thousand nirabbudas,
thirty-six and five abbudas,
such is the time that one who reviles the noble ones goes to hell.
Having formed an evil intention in speech and mind,
one who speaks what is untrue goes to hell; as does he who,
having done a deed, says, "I did not do it."
Both of those men, having passed away,
become equal in the next world— those base-doers among humans.
He who harbors malice toward a person who is free from malice...
To the pure person who is free from blemish,
that very evil returns,
like fine dust thrown against the wind.
One who is devoted to the quality of greed reviles others with his speech;
he is faithless, miserly, and ungenerous.
He was stingy and devoted to slander.
He was foul-mouthed, depraved, and ignoble;
a destroyer of living beings, wicked, and a doer of evil deeds.
O man, you are at the end of your time, born into misfortune;
do not speak much here, for you are destined for hell.
You are scattering dust upon yourself to your own detriment.
O you who blame the virtuous, doer of evil deeds:
having practiced many forms of misconduct,
you shall indeed go to the abyss for a long time.
For no one's karma ever perishes;
what is done returns to the doer alone.
The fool suffers misery in the world beyond.
The doer of evil sees it within himself:
he approaches the place struck by iron spikes and the sharp-edged iron stake.
Then there is food resembling glowing balls of iron;
even such things they call "delicious," though those who speak do not truly speak of what is pleasing.
They do not find refuge nor do they attain protection;
they lie upon glowing coals and enter into a blazing fire.
And being covered by a net,
they are struck there with iron hammers;
they enter as if into blind darkness.
For that [hell] is spread out like a vast expanse of mist.
Then they enter an iron cauldron, blazing with fire.
For they are cooked within them for a long time,
tossing about in those [fires] that are like flames;
then, amidst the mixture of pus and blood,
Therein, what does the evildoer cook?
Whichever direction he lies down toward,
there he suffers as he comes into contact with it.
In that abode of worms, amidst the waters,
what does the evildoer cook there?
For he has no hope of reaching the shore.
For all hells have surrounding moats;
but the Forest of Sword-leaves is sharp,
and they enter it with their limbs being cut to pieces.
Having seized the tongue with a hook,
they strike it again and again. Then there is also the difficult-to-cross Vetaraṇī river.
They encounter blades with sharp edges and sharp points;
there the dull-witted fall,
having committed evil deeds as evildoers.
For there, jackals, crows, and flocks of ravens devour them while they weep;
so too do greedy dogs and jackals.
Hawks and crows peck at him.
Alas, what a miserable livelihood this is for a person who touches upon evil deeds!
Therefore, while there is still life remaining here,
a person should perform what is to be done and not be negligent;
those who have been reckoned by the wise are as numerous as the seeds of sesame in a cartload.
Those who have been led to the Paduma hell number five nahutas and one hundred and twelve koṭis more.
As long as these hells of suffering are described here,
for that long must one dwell even there;
therefore, [one should strive] for the qualities of the pure, gentle, and virtuous.
“Always guard one’s speech and mind.
Thus ends the tenth discourse, the Kokālika Sutta.
